segments.text: Greek artists also told the story of Pandora's making. The ancient traveler Pausanias wrote that her birth was shown in relief on the base of the great statue of Athena inside the Parthenon. The statue itself is lost. But this small copy from Roman times still carries a version of that scene on its base.

segments.text: So where did the box come from? The change is usually traced to the early 1500s, more than two thousand years after Hesiod. The Dutch scholar Erasmus retold the story in Latin, in his famous collection of proverbs, the Adages. In this edition, printed in Venice in 1508, where Hesiod had pithos, a great jar, Erasmus wrote pyxis, a small box. And in his retelling, it is Epimetheus, not Pandora, who opens it.

segments.text: Erasmus's book was read across Europe. Later artists gave Pandora many kinds of containers: caskets, chests, and vessels. Some still showed a great jar, like this print from the 1500s. But over time, the box became the familiar image, and "Pandora's box" became an everyday phrase in English, for something that brings many troubles once it is opened.
